haiku-low.q1: They see the generic message "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
haiku-low.q2: Nothing is created or sent. They see the same generic message, since three or more rows exist in the past hour.
haiku-low.q3: It works for 30 minutes. It ends sooner when used, or when a newer link is issued for the account.
haiku-low.q4: It stays usable: used_at is not set, the token is untouched, and the user can retry until it expires.
haiku-low.q5: No devices stay logged in; all sessions are deleted, including the resetting device. The user must log in again at the login page.
haiku-low.q6: The worker retries 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. The user is not told; they see only the generic message.
haiku-low.q7: The raw token is generated as 32 random bytes and put into the emailed link, and the queued job carries it. Only its hash is stored.
haiku-low.q8: It hashes the token and looks up the reset_tokens row by token_hash. It is good only if the row exists, used_at is unset, and expires_at is after now.
haiku-low.q9: It is not kept in a separate counter; it is counted from reset_tokens rows with created_at in the last hour. Old rows fall out of the window by time.
haiku-low.q10: Their unused tokens get used_at set to now, in the same transaction as inserting the new row, before commit. Earlier links are invalidated then.
haiku-low.q11: In one transaction: used_at is set, password_hash is updated, and all the user's sessions are deleted. The confirmation email is queued only after commit.
haiku-low.q12: The conditional UPDATE (used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now) lets only one request update a row. The loser updates 0 rows, rolls back, and sees the expired page.

sonnet.q1: They see "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
sonnet.q2: The count of tokens created in the last hour is already 3 or more, so nothing is created and nothing is sent. The same generic message is shown.
sonnet.q3: 30 minutes from creation (expires_at = now + 30 min). It ends sooner if it is used, or if a newer link is requested (which sets used_at on the old one).
sonnet.q4: Unchanged and still usable. The token is untouched and the user can retry until it expires.
sonnet.q5: None. All of the user's sessions rows are deleted, including the device that did the reset. The user is not auto-logged in. They are redirected to the login page and log in with the new password.
sonnet.q6: The worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. The user is not told. They see the generic message, the attempt still counts toward the 3-per-hour limit, and they can request again.
sonnet.q7: The raw token is generated (32 random bytes) at request time. It is put in the link https://<app>/reset?token=<token> inside the queue job, queued after commit, and the email worker sends it. Only the hash is stored in the database.
sonnet.q8: It hashes the token and looks up the reset_tokens row by token_hash. The link is invalid if the row is missing, used_at is set, or expires_at <= now. Otherwise it shows the choose-a-new-password page.
sonnet.q9: There is no separate counter. It is computed by counting the user's reset_tokens rows where created_at > now - 1h. Old requests drop out when their created_at is older than an hour. Replaced and used links still count.
sonnet.q10: The user's unused tokens get used_at = now. This happens inside the same DB transaction as inserting the new token, after the limit check passes and before the insert.
sonnet.q11: In one transaction: reset_tokens.used_at is set (conditional UPDATE), users.password_hash is updated, and all of the user's sessions rows are deleted. The "password was changed" email is queued after the commit.
sonnet.q12: The conditional UPDATE (WHERE token_hash = ? AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now) in the transaction. Only one request updates 1 row. The other updates 0 rows, rolls back and gets the "expired" page.
